segments.say: In January 1962, at a girls' boarding school in the village of Kashasha, near Lake Victoria in what was then Tanganyika and is now Tanzania, a few pupils began to laugh and couldn't stop. Over the following weeks, the laughter spread through the school. It's become one of the most famous strange stories in the history of laughter, and it's often told wrongly.

The main source is a report published in 1963 by two doctors, A. M. Rankin and P. J. Philip. They described what happened at the school and in the surrounding area. According to their report, the attacks of laughing, often mixed with crying and restlessness, affected many of the pupils, and lasted from a few hours to many days in each person.

show.who: A. M. Rankin and P. J. Philip
show.what: An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika

segments.say: Their report gives the numbers. Ninety-five of the school's 159 pupils were affected, and the school had to close in March of that year. When the pupils went home, the episodes appeared in some of their villages too, and other schools in the region were affected. Over the following months, the outbreaks gradually faded away.

It's important to say clearly what this was not. It wasn't an epidemic of fun. The people affected weren't happily amused. The reports describe laughter mixed with crying, fear and distress, and people who were frightened by what was happening to them. Calling it a laughter epidemic can make it sound comic. For those who lived through it, it was not.

Doctors found no infection or poison to explain it. Most researchers who have studied the episode since describe it as a case of what's called mass psychogenic illness: real physical symptoms that spread through a group under stress, without any infectious cause. The symptoms are real, not imagined. They simply come from the mind and body under pressure, rather than from a germ.

Some researchers have pointed out that this happened at a time of great change. Tanganyika had just become independent, at the end of 1961, and many young people were facing new pressures and expectations, at school and at home. That kind of stress, some have suggested, may have helped set the stage. But it's hard to know for sure, decades later.

Wide calm water at dusk, with low green hills on the far shore and a few small fishing boats resting near the bank. It's a quiet picture of a lake region, a reminder that the story we've just heard happened to real people, in real villages, with lives that went on long after the outbreaks faded.

What does it tell us about laughter? It's an extreme, unusual example of something we've seen all evening: that laughter and other emotional behaviour can spread between people. Most of the time, that contagion is gentle and pleasant, like the couple at the next table. In rare situations of intense stress, it can become something frightening and hard to stop.

It's worth being careful not to make too much of it, though. Episodes like this are rare, and they're complicated, involving culture, stress, beliefs and group dynamics as well as laughter. They aren't a sign that ordinary contagious laughter is dangerous. They're a reminder that human beings are deeply connected, in our feelings and our bodies, sometimes more than we realise.

So here's what we can say. It began at a girls' boarding school in 1962. The laughter was mixed with crying, restlessness and fear. Doctors found no infection or poison. Most researchers see it as mass psychogenic illness, a stress response that spread through a group. And it's rare, complex, and nothing to joke about.

show.title: What we can say about Kashasha
items: It began at a girls' school in 1962
Laughing was mixed with crying and fear
It's seen as mass psychogenic illness

segments.say: Back on the quiet street, Nadia thinks about all of this, and then about the couple at the next table tonight, laughing along without knowing why. That gentle, everyday contagion is what most of us know best. It spreads warmth rather than fear. It makes strangers smile at each other. It's the same human connectedness, in its kindest form.

Looking back over the evening, Nadia can see laughter as a thread running through her whole life. Her first laughs as a baby, with her parents. The tickle monster. The pigeon in the assembly. University nights with the friends she saw tonight. Her pupils laughing during music lessons. And tonight, a teapot lid. It's been there all along, quietly holding things together.

So, why do we laugh? We've gathered a lot of pieces. Laughter seems to have begun as a play signal, millions of years ago. It's mostly social, tied far more to people than to jokes. It spreads. It helps bind friends and couples. It can soothe the body for a while. And it can come from nerves and stress as well as from joy.

If there's one idea that ties it all together, it might be this. A laugh is a way of saying, we're together, and it's all right. That's what a young chimpanzee's panting laugh seems to say during a game of chase. It's what a baby's giggle says during peekaboo. And it's what five old friends said to each other tonight, over a teapot lid.

Nadia turns the last corner onto her own street. Her house is halfway down, a single lamp glowing in the front window where she left it on this morning. The rain has stopped altogether now. The pavement shines. And she's still, very slightly, smiling.

Before she goes in, there are a few things worth keeping from tonight. Some small, practical ideas about laughter, the kind you can carry into an ordinary day. We'll gather them up at the front door. And then, very gently, we'll begin to wind down for sleep.
